claims.text: Grain-boundary engineering can improve the mechanical properties of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary engineering refines grain size and optimizes grain-boundary structure.
Refined grain size and optimized grain-boundary structure increase hardness and strength.
The applicable initial material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state.
Thermomechanical processing can be used to engineer grain boundaries in this alloy.
Alloying-element additions can be used to engineer grain boundaries in this alloy.
The proposed testing conditions are room-temperature, uniaxial mechanical-property and deformation tests.
Grain size and grain-boundary structure are the structural mediators of the proposed property changes.
Refined grains and optimized grain boundaries produce grain-boundary strengthening.
Increased dislocation density and grain-boundary strengthening improve hardness and strength.
Grain-boundary engineering will increase yield strength by 10–20% relative to the starting state.
Grain-boundary engineering will increase hardness by 5–10% relative to the starting state.
The baseline is an as-cast or annealed equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
The exact relationship between grain-boundary structure and mechanical properties is not well understood.
Failure to obtain a significant increase in both yield strength and hardness after grain-boundary engineering would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits unspecified alloying-element additions, while the boundary restricts applicability to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi. Additions could change the composition or introduce another element and therefore move the treated material outside the stated boundary.
